clusters.name: Teodor's death, 1978–1979
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather Teodor's death in January 1978, within the following year: your grandmother Delphine stopped cooking and went to your mother's every evening; your father took night shifts and distanced from your mother; your uncle Anton drank at lunch and was warned at work; his wife Celeste left with their child in August; your mother's anxiety rose over her mother and Anton; your brother Callum had ear infections through the winter; your grandmother took a job at the library by May 1979. The shifts pile up across the family in these months, each one's move near another's.

1984: Your mother's bed rest in March is a shift in functioning; your grandmother Hazel came to overfunction in April; your father and Hazel argued in May; your brother Callum stammered again in June; and your sister Ines was born in September. The opening event marking a change in the family is your mother's bed rest, but one of the five supporting shifts is marked neverOpens (your anxiety about your father at your bedside), leaving four shifts that count. Your mother's functioning down at the start opens the period, but the shift itself, not a change in who is in the family or how a key member functions, cannot open a period, so not enough in the diagram to choose a reading.

1986–1997: Your grandmother Hazel was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in September 1986, a real threat to how she could function. The events that follow show your grandfather Ambrose overfunctioning in her care, your father's anxiety rising as he phoned nightly for news, Hazel's own functioning falling through falls and medicines, Ambrose's functioning declining as he gave up his workshop, conflict between your parents over your father's time at his parents' house, and your uncle Lyle's distance from his parents. After Hazel moved to the Fairlie nursing home in June 1997 and your father cut back his drinking by October, the family settled into a new balance. This is your grandmother's long decline, and the shifts are hers and her family's reactions across eleven years, but your own shifts during these years (sleeping and schooling in 1984, and your work and functioning from 1999 onward) fall outside this run of events, so the period covers the family's reactions to her illness and is not about you.

1999–2000: Your brother Callum left home for work up north in May 1999. Around this event: your father and Callum argued over his plans; your mother's anxiety rose at the thought of him far away; your father missed work and sat in the garage; your sister Ines skipped school; your mother took Ines everywhere with her; and by August 2000 Ines was back at school full days and passed her exams. The opening event is your brother leaving home. Your own shifts do not show in these months—you were away at college—so the period holds only the family's reactions to Callum's departure, and no shifts of yours.

2003: Your grandmother Hazel died in January; within the following months, you could not sleep, stopped going to the bookshop and lost the job by May, stopped returning your mother's calls, and dreaded buses and crowded shops. By November you took a job at the garden centre and slept through the night again. This is your own period in response to her death, the one you named; it is held under your answer, not here.

2005-11-19 to 2005-11-23: Your sister Ines slid off the road on black ice on 19 November and spent two nights in hospital with a cracked rib. Within these four days: your mother sat up all night by the phone; your father could not keep food down; your brother Callum came down from the north overnight to her bedside; Ines shook at the thought of the ride home; and by 23 November your mother was calm again once Ines was home and up and about. All shifts fall within the same few days around a real threat, and the family settled within days: an acute episode, not a period.
